1:
With the very first words the writer names himself and his moment, and the witnesses divide their attention between the man and the place. The reformed John Gill observes that the Hebrew rendered “the words of Nehemiah” signifies things done as well as things spoken, so that the title promises a record of transactions and deeds; who his father Hachaliah was cannot now be known, and the Arabic addition that he was the high priest rests on no foundation. Some, Gill notes, have thought Nehemiah himself a priest — partly from the account in the Second Book of Maccabees that has him offer sacrifice, partly from his sealing the covenant at the head of the priests — but he judges him rather of the tribe of Judah, perhaps the same Nehemiah who had gone up with Zerubbabel, returned, and become the king’s cupbearer.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same title and reach the same sense. In the headings of prophetic books the word means discourses, the announcement of God’s word; but in historical writing — as with the recorded acts of David in 1 Chron. 29:29, of Solomon, and of Jeroboam — it denotes deeds and experiences, so that “the words of Nehemiah” is simply the history of Nehemiah.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry fixes on Nehemiah’s station. He was in Shushan the palace, the royal city where the Persian court was kept, and — as he only lets slip at the chapter’s end — the king’s cupbearer, a place of great trust and honour. Henry marks his modesty in not being forward to tell of his preferment, and teaches us to be slow to speak of our own advancements. But he reads the providence gratefully: when God has work to do he never wants instruments; those he designs to employ he fits and calls; and he keeps his remnant in all places — an Obadiah in the house of Ahab, saints in Caesar’s household as in Phil. 4:22, a devout Nehemiah in Shushan — for God can make the courts of princes nurseries and sanctuaries to the friends of the church.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, drawing on Prideaux, sets the date: Nehemiah, who succeeded Ezra in the government, came in the twentieth year of Artaxerxes Longimanus, about 445 years before Christ; his ancestors had been citizens of Jerusalem, though his father had settled in the land of captivity, and it was likely his dwelling at Shushan, and perhaps the favour of Queen Esther, that raised him to be cupbearer, daily in the king’s presence. Clarke and Charles Ellicott together fix the calendar: the month Chisleu answers to part of our November and December, the twentieth year runs from the reign of Artaxerxes, and Shushan is Susa, the ancient winter residence of the Persian kings, the city of Daniel’s vision in Dan. 8:2 and of Ahasuerus’ feast in Esther 1:3. John Wesley adds only that “the words” are rather the acts, and Shushan the royal city of Persia.
2:
News reaches the palace by the coming of a kinsman, and the witnesses first settle who he was. The reformed John Gill allows that Hanani, called “one of my brethren,” may be a brother in nature or only a Jew of the same nation and religion, and cites Jarchi’s reading of him as one of Nehemiah’s companions or acquaintance. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch press further: though “brethren” can stretch to distant relations, since Nehemiah again names Hanani “my brother” in Neh. 7:2, his own brother is meant. Charles Ellicott agrees that Hanani was Nehemiah’s own brother and that he came “from Judah,” out of the province itself, adding that nothing is said of any errand — there is no hint that he had been sent to the Persian court on account of recent troubles.

The heart of the verse is the question Nehemiah puts, and Keil weighs its terms. “The Jews that had escaped” are those left of the captivity, those who had returned to Judah, set in deliberate contrast to the many who still remained in heathen lands; and Nehemiah’s inquiry runs to two things, the people and the city, the Jews and Jerusalem. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke supplies the scene from Josephus: Nehemiah, being somewhere outside Susa, heard strangers conversing in the Hebrew tongue, drew near, and finding them Jews come from Jerusalem asked how it fared with their brethren there and what their state was — the very substance recorded in the text, though Josephus tells it with added detail.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the enquiry as the movement of a heart that dignity could not harden. A friend and relation came to court, by whom Nehemiah had opportunity to inform himself fully how it went with the children of the captivity and in what posture Jerusalem, the beloved city, then lay. Though he lived at ease, in honour and fulness, he could not forget that he was an Israelite, nor shake off the thoughts of his brethren in distress; like Moses in Acts 7:23, he in spirit visited them and looked upon their burdens. Neither the dignity to which he was advanced, nor the difference of their practice — for they had returned while he stayed and conformed to the court — alienated his affection; he did not judge or despise them, but kindly concerned himself, and, that he might know how to do them a kindness, asked concerning them. It is lawful and good, Henry adds, to inquire “What news?” — especially concerning the state of the church and religion — not, like the Athenians who spent their time in nothing but to tell or hear some new thing in Acts 17:21, merely to have something to talk of, but that we may know how to direct our prayers and our praises.
3:
The answer comes freighted with grief, and the witnesses take it in two parts, the people and the city. The reformed John Gill fixes “there in the province” as Judea, now reduced to a mere province of the Persian empire. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the pathos in the very words: those who had returned are called in the question “the Jews that had escaped” and in the answer “the remnant that are left,” both drawn from the captivity; their “great affliction and reproach” is the distress of a despised people under the contempt of the neighbours around them, language familiar in the prophets but here combined in a peculiarly affecting way.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry notes that Hanani, of whom it is later said that he feared God above many in Neh. 7:2, would speak not only truly but tenderly of Jerusalem’s desolations. The account is twofold: the holy seed was trampled and abused, insulted by its neighbours and filled with the scorn of those at ease; and the holy city lay exposed, its wall broken down and its gates as the Chaldeans had left them. The temple was built, the government settled, a work of reformation brought to some head — yet here was one good work still undone; and every Jerusalem on this side the heavenly one, Henry reflects, will have some defect for the making up of which it needs the help of its friends.

Over the ruined wall the witnesses divide. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues that it must refer to walls rebuilt after the return from captivity, since to hear of the ruin left by Nebuchadnezzar could be no news to Nehemiah at all. Against this, John Wesley reads the report plainly: the walls and gates continue as Nebuchadnezzar left them, the Jews neither being in a condition to rebuild them nor having commission from the Persian kings to do so. Ellicott holds with Wesley — the walls were still lying prostrate, with partial exceptions, as Nebuchadnezzar left them a hundred and forty-two years before, as recorded in 2 Kings 25:10, and the burning of the gates, though not previously set down, belongs to that same ancient overthrow; there is no valid reason, he insists, to suppose the walls had been partly restored and again demolished. Keil and Delitzsch report that opinions are indeed divided — some older expositors held for a recent demolition by hostile neighbours — but note Rambach’s reply that Scripture tells us nothing of any rebuilding of the wall by Zerubbabel or Ezra which such a demolition would presuppose. Thus the report itself becomes the seed of the whole book: a city whose worship was restored but whose walls still lay in the dust.
4:
The tidings break the hearer, and the witnesses watch how a courtier’s grief turns Godward. The reformed John Gill marks simply that it was this sad and melancholy account that so moved him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry dwells on the depth and the direction of the sorrow. Nehemiah did not merely weep in a passion when the news first came; his grief continued certain days, for the desolations and distresses of the church ought to be matter of our grief however much we ourselves live at ease. And he fasted and prayed — not in public, for he had no opportunity of that, but before the God of heaven who sees in secret and will reward openly.

By his fasting and praying, Henry says, Nehemiah consecrated his sorrows and directed his tears aright, sorrowing after a godly sort with an eye to God, whose name was reproached in the contempt cast upon his people; he eased his sorrows and unburdened his spirit by pouring out his complaint before God and leaving it with him; and he took the right method of fetching in relief for his people and direction for himself. Let those who are forming any good design for the public, Henry counsels, take God along with them for the very first conception of it, and utter all their projects before him; this is the way to prosper in them.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke measures the length of the mourning. Nehemiah mourned “certain days” — from the month Chisleu to the month Nisan, about four months from the time he received this information until Artaxerxes noticed his sadness in Neh. 2:1 — and all this time he probably spent in supplication, waiting for a favourable opening in the divine providence. From this Clarke draws a caution: every good work is not to be undertaken hastily; prayer and watchfulness are necessary to its completion, and many good works have been ruined by making haste. John Wesley adds only a word on the title “the God of heaven,” the God who sees in secret, before whom Nehemiah mourned, having no opportunity of doing it openly. The witnesses converge on a single picture: a man high in a heathen court, with every earthly reason for contentment, who hears of a broken city far away and cannot rest — who makes of his grief not a complaint but a prayer, and of his fasting the patient antechamber to action.
5:
The prayer opens with a name, and the witnesses linger over the God to whom it is addressed. The reformed John Gill notes first what Nehemiah did not do: he prayed not to the host of heaven, nor to the sun which the Persians adored, but to the God of heaven, and that in humble supplication. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch hear in each title a strand of covenant theology: “God of heaven” alludes to God’s almighty government of the world; “the great and terrible God” recalls the language of Deut. 7:21; and “who keepest covenant and mercy for them that love him” echoes both Deut. 7:9 and the second commandment of Exod. 20:6. The prayer that follows, they add, gathers up the supplications Nehemiah had been making day and night through all his mourning.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the address a whole pattern for drawing near to God, and observes that it is much the same as Daniel’s confession in Dan. 9:4. We are to come, first, with a holy awe of God’s majesty and glory — remembering that he is the God of heaven, infinitely above us and sovereign over us, the great and terrible God who excels all the principalities and powers of the upper and lower worlds, angels and kings alike, and is to be worshipped with fear; even the terrors of the Lord, Henry notes, are improvable for the comfort and encouragement of those who trust in him. And we are to come, second, with a holy confidence in his grace and truth, for he keeps covenant and mercy for those who love him — not merely the mercy he promised, but even more than he promised, since nothing shall be thought too much to be done for those who love him and keep his commandments.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the titles as the pre-exilic “Jehovah, God of hosts” confessed afresh: “great,” as able to do mighty things, and “terrible,” as able to inflict the heaviest judgments. The witnesses do not divide. Gill guards the object of the prayer against the idolatry all around it; Keil traces each epithet to its root in the law; Henry turns the invocation into a lesson in reverent boldness; Clarke weighs the power the names confess. Together they show a man who, before he asks anything, steadies himself upon the character of God — almighty to save and dreadful to offend, yet bound by his own covenant to those who love him — and so lays the only sure foundation for the confession and the petition that follow.
6:
Having named his God, Nehemiah begs to be heard, and the witnesses attend to the intensity of the plea. The reformed John Gill takes the opening simply as a cry that God’s ear be attentive to the prayer now made. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that “let thine ear be attentive, and thine eyes open” is the very language of Solomon’s temple prayer in 2 Chron. 6:40 and its answer in 2 Chron. 7:15; that the word our version renders “this day” means rather “now,” at this time, as the added “day and night” confirms, since the mourning had already lasted many days; and that Nehemiah, to press home his sense of guilt, moves from the communal “which we have sinned” to the personal “both I and my father’s house have sinned.”

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs both the request and the confession. On the request he is exact: Nehemiah asks God to be attentive not to the prayer he says — for barely saying a prayer will not serve — but to the prayer he prays; we are likely to speed in praying, Henry remarks, only when we pray in praying. And he asks that God’s eyes be open upon the heart from which the prayer comes and the case laid before him: he who formed the eye and planted the ear shall surely see clearly and hear attentively.

On the confession Henry marks the humility of it. It is no great mortification to own that Israel has sinned; but Nehemiah says, “I and my father’s house have sinned,” taking shame to himself and numbering himself among the guilty. In true confession, Henry adds, two things must be owned as the malignity of sin — that it is a corruption of ourselves and an affront to God. The witnesses converge on the same note of self-implicating honesty: Gill and Keil fix the plain sense and the grammar of the appeal, while Henry draws from it the difference between saying prayers and praying them, and between a general acknowledgment that the nation has failed and a penitent’s willingness to write his own name and his own house first among the offenders. It is the mark of Nehemiah’s intercession throughout that he never stands apart from those he pleads for: their guilt is his guilt, and the confession he makes for Israel he makes, without reserve, for himself. And Keil marks that this was no passing remorse but the burden of many days: the prayer here recorded gathers up what Nehemiah had poured out before God day and night, so that the confession is a settled grief carried steadily to the throne.
7:
The confession grows specific, naming the law that had been broken. The reformed John Gill reads “we have dealt very corruptly against thee” as a corrupting of God’s covenant, laws, and precepts, as well as of themselves and their own ways — all of it against the Lord, contrary to his nature, mind, and will. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the grammar of the verb, an infinitive of intensity, and gloss the phrase: to deal corruptly against God is precisely to have failed to keep the commandments, the statutes, and the judgments of his law.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke distinguishes the three terms Nehemiah heaps together. The commandments are the moral precepts by which our lives are to be regulated; the statutes are what pertains to the rites and ceremonies of religion; the judgments are the precepts of justice that govern our conduct toward one another. By naming all three, Nehemiah confesses a breach that ran through the whole law — moral, ceremonial, and civil alike.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the malignity of the sin into two heads. Sin is first a corruption of ourselves, and second an affront to God; to deal corruptly against God is to set up the corruptions of our own hearts in direct opposition to his commands. And Henry marks the honesty with which Nehemiah owns the charge: he does not say only that Israel had not kept the judgments God commanded his servant Moses, but confesses “we have not kept” them, ranging himself and his father’s house within the indictment. Yet even here, Henry observes, the confession is laying the ground of a plea; the same Moses to whom the commandments were given is the Moses to whom the promise was given, and Nehemiah, having owned that they had not kept what God commanded, will presently beg God to remember what God himself had spoken. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the breadth of the corruption, against God’s very nature; Keil ties the corrupt dealing to the unkept law; Clarke sorts the commandments, statutes, and judgments into their several kinds; Henry names the double malignity of sin and the honesty of a confession that spares no one, least of all the man who makes it. For Nehemiah the point of owning the breach so fully is not to sink into despair but to prepare the way; a sin unconfessed cannot be forgiven, and only the prayer that first tells the whole truth about the transgression can go on to plead the promise that meets it.
8:
The prayer turns from confession to a plea grounded on God’s own word. The reformed John Gill notes that Nehemiah asks God to remember the word he had commanded Moses to publish and declare to the children of Israel. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch unfold the whole structure of the plea: with his confession of grievous transgression Nehemiah combines the petition that God would be mindful of the word declared through Moses — that if his people, scattered among the heathen for their sins, should turn to him and keep his commandments, he would gather them from the most distant regions and bring them back to the place he had chosen to set his name. This word Nehemiah designates as one God had commanded to Moses, since it formed part of the covenant law prescribed as Israel’s rule of life; and its matter runs, if ye transgress, I will scatter you among the nations.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces the citation to its sources in the law — the warnings of Lev. 26:33 and of Deut. 4:27 and Deut. 28:64 — and draws a lesson from Nehemiah’s accuracy: though he was in an enemy’s country and far from the ordinances of God, he had not forgotten the law, but had read his Bible well and quoted it correctly.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry shows how the threat itself becomes a plea. God had said that if they broke covenant with him he would scatter them among the nations, and that threatening had been fulfilled in the captivity — never was a people so widely dispersed as Israel, though at first so closely incorporated. Nehemiah takes hold of the very word of judgment because the same word carried a promise beyond it, drawn from Deut. 30:1, that if they turned to God he would gather them again; and now, Henry notes, they had begun to turn, having renounced idolatry and kept to the temple service. So Nehemiah begs God to remember that word — not because the Eternal Mind needs a remembrancer, but because it was the ground on which he built his faith. “Lord, remember the word,” he prays, though he had just owned, “we have not kept the word”; and Henry draws the comfort of it: if God were not more mindful of his promises than we are of his precepts, we should be undone. Our best pleas in prayer, he concludes, are always those taken from the promise of God, the word on which he has caused us to hope in Ps. 119:49.
9:
The promised turn of mercy is now spelled out, and the witnesses follow its reach. The reformed John Gill reads “if ye return unto me” as a returning by repentance, proved genuine by a yielding and continuing obedience to God’s commands. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence to its farthest horizon: though there were of the scattered people cast out to the uttermost part of the heaven, God would gather them even from thence and bring them to the place he had chosen to set his name there. And they observe how the prayer now widens to take in more than Nehemiah alone: it closes with the reiterated entreaty that God would hearken to the prayer of his servant and of his servants together — all those Israelites who, like him, delight to fear God’s name and pray for their people’s redemption.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the condition and the comfort of it. God had indeed said he would scatter a covenant-breaking people, and it was done; but he had said too that if they turned to him — as now, renouncing idolatry and holding to the temple worship, they had begun to do — he would gather them again, and this from the promise of Deut. 30:4, where the outcasts in the uttermost parts of heaven are named for the very purpose of being brought home. The distance is put in to magnify the mercy: no dispersion is too wide for the God who chose a place to set his name. Henry hears in the whole plea a man guiding his own desires by God’s rule and grounding his faith and hope upon God’s word, laying that word before God as the reason of his asking.

The witnesses converge. Gill fixes the reality of the repentance the promise requires; Keil traces the sweep of the ingathering and the company of praying servants the verse gathers in; Henry finds in it the pattern of a prayer that asks nothing God has not first promised. Together they show that Nehemiah’s confidence for a scattered and defenceless remnant rests wholly on the settled word of God — a word that had threatened dispersion and now pledged return — so that even from the ends of the heavens the people whom judgment had flung abroad might be gathered to the one place where the Lord had set his name. The mercy is not wrung from a reluctant God but claimed from a faithful one, whose own word had appointed both the scattering and the gathering.
10:
The plea passes from the promise to the people it concerns, and the witnesses mark how Nehemiah presses the relation. The reformed John Gill identifies “thy servants and thy people” as those gathered out of several countries and returned to Jerusalem and Judah — a people scattered among the nations for their sins, yet still owned by God as his own servants and his own portion, the very remnant whose affliction had first set Nehemiah weeping. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the words within the prayer’s closing movement, where Nehemiah, having rehearsed the covenant word, now lays hold of the people as God’s own, redeemed by his great power and his strong hand.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the verse a double argument drawn from what Israel was to God. First he pleads the relation: these are thy servants and thy people, whom thou hast set apart for thyself and taken into covenant with thee; and will God suffer his sworn enemies to trample and oppress his sworn servants? If he will not appear for his own people, Henry asks with the prophet, for whom will he appear, recalling the cry of Isa. 63:19. Then he pleads the great things already done: “whom thou hast redeemed by thy great power” in the days of old. That power, Henry urges, is still the same; the God who once brought them out of Egypt with a strong hand can surely redeem them still, and those who have a God of infinite power on their side need not be overpowered by the enemy. The redemption of old is thus made the earnest of redemption to come, and the covenant into which they were taken the reason why they may not now be cast off.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the identity of the redeemed remnant; Keil sets the appeal within the prayer’s final entreaty; Henry builds from Israel’s covenant standing and its ancient ransom a ground on which present mercy may be begged. Together they show Nehemiah pressing upon God the bonds God himself had formed — servants he had chosen, a people he had ransomed by a mighty hand — as if to say that the honour of the Redeemer is bound up with the rescue of the redeemed, and that a power once great enough to free them cannot now prove too small to keep them. It is the boldest ground the prayer has yet taken, and it prepares for the single personal petition with which the whole confession will close.
11:
The long confession narrows at last to a single, personal request, and the witnesses gather at the point where prayer turns toward action. The reformed John Gill takes the renewed cry — “let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant” — as Nehemiah pressing home the very petition he had been making all this while. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note how the prayer widens and then sharpens: God is asked to hear his servant and his servants together, all those who delight to fear his name, before Nehemiah adds the one thing he wants for himself — “prosper thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man.”

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads “mercy in the sight of this man” as favour before the king, and thinks the words a silent, inward prayer offered in the very moment Nehemiah was handing the cup into the royal hand — for, as the closing clause reveals, “I was the king’s cupbearer.” That office, Clarke explains, was one of great trust: the king’s butler, whom the Persians called the saky, stood daily in the royal presence, and no Eastern potentate would keep near him a cupbearer he could not trust with his life, since poison was so readily given in the cup. John Wesley reads the same clause to the same effect: the place gave Nehemiah both opportunity to speak to the king and some favour with him. And Wesley marks the phrase “this man” — the king, for all his greatness, is but a man, and his heart therefore wholly at God’s disposal; favour with men, he adds, is comfortable only when we see it springing from the mercy of God. On “who desire to fear thy name” Wesley notes the gracious rule: those who truly desire to fear his name shall be graciously accepted of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers these threads. The petition is that God would prosper Nehemiah and give him favour with the king; and he calls him simply “this man,” for the greatest of men are but men before God — “who art thou, that thou shouldest be afraid of a man?” in the sense of Ps. 9:20. The mercy Nehemiah seeks in the sight of this man is not, Henry insists, the king’s mercy but mercy from God in his approach to the king; favour with men is then truly comfortable when we can trace it to the mercy of God. And the desire to fear God’s name, which Nehemiah pleads on behalf of all God’s servants, Henry reads as the very mark God accepts, for such a desire is his own work in the soul. So the prayer that began by naming the God of heaven ends by naming a man, and asks that the almighty compassion just invoked would go before Nehemiah into the throne-room and dispose a king’s heart toward a broken city — closing not in despair over Jerusalem’s ruin but in quiet expectation that mercy sought in secret will be answered in the sight of men.
